title: Here am I; send me (Isaiah 6:1–8)
hookLine: seraphim, a live coal on the lips, and a prophet who volunteers

cards: "In the year that king Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and His train filled the temple." Isaiah dates the vision by a death.

A king is gone, and in the Temple a man sees something that fills the whole space. Above the throne stand seraphim, burning ones, each with six wings: two to cover the face, two to cover the feet, two to fly.
And they are calling to one another.

teach.b: What they call is this: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; The whole earth is full of His glory." You may have heard it in a synagogue.
It's at the heart of the Kedushah, said during the leader's repetition of the Amidah, when people rise up on their toes at each holy. The doorposts shake. Smoke fills the house.

teach.h: WOE IS ME, A MAN OF UNCLEAN LIPS.
teach.b: And Isaiah's first words aren't brave at all: "Woe is me! for I am undone; Because I am a man of unclean lips, And I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips". He feels too small and too stained for the room.

teach.h: A LIVE COAL TOUCHES HIS LIPS.
teach.b: Then one of the seraphim takes a live coal from the altar with tongs, flies to him, and touches his mouth: "Lo, this hath touched thy lips; And thine iniquity is taken away".

The lips he was ashamed of are the ones cleansed, the very place a prophet will work. Then Isaiah hears a voice, not addressed to him, a question into the room: "Whom shall I send, And who will go for us?"
And he answers: "Here am I; send me." In Hebrew, the first word is hineni. Abraham says hineni when God calls him by name.
So does Moses at the burning bush. But they were called by name. Isaiah wasn't.
He heard an open question and stepped forward, and said yes before he heard the job. The task that follows is a hard one, as the very next verses show. Hineni is not a promise that it'll be easy.
It's a person saying: I'm here, I'm listening, use me.

how: Jews say the seraphim's words, 'holy, holy, holy', in the Kedushah during the repetition of the Amidah, and it is a custom to rise on the toes at each 'holy'.

o: here I am: ready, listening, willing to be sent
woe is me: a cry that you're unworthy
holy, holy, holy: the call of the seraphim

games.q: here am I — tap the pairs.

s: God called Isaiah by name before he answered
he heard an open question, whom shall I send, and volunteered.
Isaiah's first reaction was woe is me
he said he was a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips.
the seraphim's words are said in Jewish prayer
holy, holy, holy is at the heart of the Kedushah.

games.q: you're in the Temple. you've just been cleansed by a live coal, and you hear: whom shall I send? what do you say?
o: nothing; the question wasn't for me.
first tell me what the job is.
games.why: Isaiah answers here am I; send me, before he hears what the task will be.

practice: Listen for the open questions around you that nobody's answering: who can drive, who'll bring food, who'll sit with her?
If a voice in you says, like Isaiah, I'm not good enough for this, breathe through it, and quietly try the word: hineni, here I am. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Hineni. "Here I am": Isaiah's answer to an open question in the Temple, given before he knew the task. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: here I am, the word Abraham, Moses and Isaiah answer with.

carryVoice: Your line: here am I, send me. Said before he even knew the task. Rest well.
